title: Every one had a name
hook: Yad Vashem gathers the name of every victim it can

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith after, and your line: every answer is honored. Did you listen to someone without correcting them? Today the week comes to rest, on names. Day one thousand twenty-two.

On Yom HaShoah, Israel's day of Holocaust remembrance, people step up to microphones in the Knesset, in schools, in synagogues, and read names aloud. One name. Then another. Then the next. A grandmother. A cousin no one else remembers. A child. Sometimes a reader adds a town, or a word about who the person was. The reading doesn't summarize. It doesn't round anything off. It just keeps going, one person at a time. Today's line is the idea underneath that reading.
screen: `NAMES READ ALOUD.` → `ONE, THEN ANOTHER.` → `NOTHING ROUNDED OFF.`

segments.voice: Israel's Holocaust memorial takes its name from the prophet Isaiah. There, God speaks to people who feared they would leave no children to carry their name, and promises them, in the Hebrew, a yad vashem: a monument and a memorial, literally a hand and a name. The same verse goes on: "I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off." Yad Vashem has spent its life gathering names. One of its tools is plain: the Page of Testimony. A single sheet for a single person. A relative or a friend writes down a name, a town, the names of parents, a job, what is known about how they died, and sometimes attaches a photograph. The pages are kept in the Hall of Names, and the gathering goes on, because some names are still missing. The Israeli poet Zelda wrote a poem about this, in paraphrase: every person has a name, given by God, by parents, by the way they stood and smiled, by the work they did, by the people who loved them. The name-reading ceremonies take their title from it. Now look back at this week. Fighters in the Warsaw ghetto. The Trocmés, Chiune Sugihara, Irena Sendler. Hannah Senesh. Soldiers at the gates, and the people they found. Witnesses who told. Survivors who prayed, or argued, or stopped. All of it comes down, in the end, to persons. Not a number. Each one had a name.
screen: `A HAND AND A NAME.` · `AN EVERLASTING NAME.` · `ONE PAGE FOR ONE PERSON.` · `EVERY ONE HAD A NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one name aloud. Choose one. It might be a name from this week, like Hannah Senesh or Irena Sendler. It might be someone from your own family. Say it out loud, slowly, once. Then sit with it. Not a statistic, not a category. A person who answered to that name when someone called it across a room. If you pray, you can hold that name in your prayer. If you don't, just let it stay in the air of the room with you. Later, if you'd like, look up one name in Yad Vashem's online database. The bell holds the time.
Yad Vashem. Hebrew for a hand and a name: Israel's Holocaust memorial, and its work of gathering names one by one so each person is remembered. Today's word.
Your line: some names are still missing. Today, learn one name and one detail about one person who was lost, and say both out loud. Day one thousand twenty-two.

howItsDone: On Yom HaShoah, communities in Israel and elsewhere hold name-reading ceremonies, and families fill in Pages of Testimony at Yad Vashem for relatives who were murdered.
